name: Southeast Babar
confidence_why: The only description of Southeast Babar phonology, Steinhauer (2009), states from his own fieldwork that stress is not phonemic at the word level and that the same word is heard with different stress in comparable environments, and no other source addresses stress.
catalog_citation: Steinhauer, Hein. 2009. The sounds of Southeast Babar. In K. Alexander Adelaar & Andrew Pawley (eds.), Austronesian historical linguistics and culture history: a festschrift for Robert Blust (Pacific Linguistics 601), 91-105. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU.
catalog_locator: p. 96, §2.2 Phonology (chapter page 6; volume page 109); fn. 26 at the foot of p. 102 (chapter file page 12)
catalog_quote: Stress does not seem to be phonemic at the word level. Often the same word occurs with different stress in comparable environments. Below I refrain with some exceptions from indicating stress. [p. 96] ... This lengthening seems to be frequent in (stressed?) monosyllabic words closed by /l/ or /m/. [p. 96] ... It seems that this change did not occur when *u was stressed. In one set of possessive enclitics, which always clearly attracted phrasal stress in Fien Laun's pronunciation, *u is preserved as u, e.g. in ox='u, ox=m'u 'my head, your (SG) head'. [fn. 26, p. 102]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened: (15 pp., text, pypdf cut) and the whole-volume file (553 pp., text). extracted text on both, no scanned needed. Verbatim check. Chapter file page 6 = running head "96 Hein Steinhauer", §2.2 Phonology, immediately after example (1) (vowel-length minimal pairs): "Stress does not seem to be phonemic at the word level. Often the same word occurs with different stress in comparable environments. Below I refrain with some exceptions from indicating stress." Exact match. Same page, vowel-length paragraph: "This lengthening seems to be frequent in (stressed?) monosyllabic words closed by /l/ or /m/." Exact match. Volume file page 109 carries the same text (checked), and volume pages 104-118…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author finds no fixed or contrastive word-level stress: the same word is heard with stress on different syllables in comparable contexts, so stress is not marked in the transcriptions except occasionally. The only stable prominence reported is phrasal: a set of possessive enclitics consistently attracts phrase stress. Stress marks that do appear in the chapter fall on various syllables (e.g. [təˈla] final, [lɛχˈwyɔrl] final, [ukˈunt] final, [bɛˈbɛrklɔl] second/penult, ['utyə] initial), consistent with the claim of variability.
new_statements.exceptions: The author marks stress 'with some exceptions'; vowel lengthening is said to be frequent in '(stressed?) monosyllabic words closed by /l/ or /m/' (author's own question mark); historically, *u was retained when stressed, i.e. in possessive enclitics that attract phrasal stress (fn. 26).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level explicitly ('at the word level'); the stable prominence noted is at phrase level (enclitic-attracted 'phrasal stress'). Data: elicited citation forms and paradigms from a single speaker (Fien Laun, b. 1958, Letwurung dialect), recorded in the Netherlands (Nijmegen field-methods course 2005; Groningen), decades after she left the community; the author flags his 'untrained ears' and that the description is preliminary 'research in progress'.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement describes the Letwurung dialect of Southeast Babar (village Letwurung, southeast coast of Babar Island), the idiolect of one speaker, Fien Laun, resident in the Netherlands since 1983. Glottolog lists no dialects under sout2883; Steinhauer's Table 1 (p. 93) places Letwurung among the Southeast Babar villages (Koroing, Letwurung..), so glottocode sout2883 applies. Ethnologue's 'Southeast Babar' [vbb] is the same entity.
